s305: Ask God to grow His fruit in you
s306: God made me, and God is still growing me.
s307: A test can tell you a little about yourself, but it can't say who you will become. You can always grow.
s308: The Pastor Who Ran Out of Words
s309: Samuel, 44, pastor of a growing church in Kottayam, Kerala
s310: Samuel loved his people. He loved preaching, praying with the sick and sitting with families in grief. But by Sunday evening he would lock himself in the bathroom just to be alone for ten minutes. Monday was meant to be his day off, yet the phone kept ringing. Weddings, funerals, committee meetings and home visits filled every week. He began to dread the knock on the door. He felt guilty, because a good pastor, he thought, should always want to be with people. His wife noticed he was short with the children and silent at dinner. One Sunday, halfway through greeting the congregation, he felt his chest tighten and his mind go blank. He smiled and shook hands, but inside he whispered, Lord, I cannot keep doing this.
s311: Research suggests introverts tend to reach their comfortable level of stimulation sooner than extroverts. Long hours of talk, noise and emotional care fill their nervous system quickly, and quiet time helps it settle again. This is not weakness or lack of love. It is partly inherited temperament, and twin studies suggest roughly 40 to 50 percent of the difference in extraversion comes from genes. Samuel had also absorbed a belief from his own father, a busy preacher, that saying no to anyone was selfish. So he ignored the early signs of tiredness until his body raised the alarm. Without regular recovery, stress hormones stay high, sleep suffers and patience wears thin. Samuel did not need to love people less. He needed to plan for how God had wired him.
s312: A retired pastor friend asked him, When did Jesus go to the mountain alone? Samuel realised Jesus withdrew often, even when crowds were waiting. He began to see rest not as escape from ministry but as part of it. Planning his recharge became an act of stewardship, not selfishness.
s313: Map which tasks drain him and which restore him
s314: Protect two quiet hours every morning for prayer and study
s315: Make Monday a true Sabbath with the phone switched off
s316: Train two elders to share home visits and hospital calls
s317: Take a short silent walk after every Sunday service
s318: Jesus Himself made space for solitude. Mark 1:35 tells us that rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed. Luke 5:16 says he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed, even as great multitudes came to hear Him. When His disciples were worn out, He said, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while (Mark 6:31). Moses nearly broke under the weight of judging the people alone until Jethro told him, Thou art not able to perform it thyself alone (Exodus 18:18). Rest and shared leadership are not signs of failure. They are God's own pattern for those who serve, so that love can keep flowing for a lifetime.
s319: God did not make every servant the same. Some are energised by crowds, others by quiet depth, and the body of Christ needs both. An introvert's nervous system notices detail, listens deeply and reflects carefully, which are gifts in counselling, prayer and preaching. The need for quiet is part of that same design. Just as a lamp needs oil, a reflective soul needs stillness to keep giving light. When we honour the limits God built into us, we stop running on guilt and start serving from fullness, trusting that He, not our endless availability, holds His church together.
s320: Mark 6:31|Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while
s324: The first months were hard. Some members complained that the pastor was less available, and Samuel felt the old guilt rise each Monday. Twice he slid back into overwork during the festival season. But with elders sharing visits and mornings protected, his sleep improved and his preaching grew richer. His wife said he laughed more at home. He still gets tired, but now he notices it early and responds.
s325: Planning your recharge is not selfishness but faithful stewardship of how God made you.
s326: Some people get tired from being with lots of people, even people they love. Taking quiet time to rest with God helps them love others well again.
s327: The Girl Who Was Called Too Much
s328: Ananya, 8, the lively youngest child in a quiet family in Pune, Maharashtra
s329: Ananya talked from the moment she woke up. She sang in the bathroom, invited the whole lane to play cricket and asked strangers on the bus their names. Her parents and older brother were all quiet people who loved books and calm evenings. At first they laughed at her energy, but slowly the laughter turned to sighs. Ananya, you are too much, her mother would say. Can you ever be quiet? her brother asked. At school her teacher wrote that she disturbed others. One evening Ananya came home and sat alone in her room, unusually silent. When her father asked what was wrong, she said, I am trying to be less of me so everyone will like me better. His heart broke. He realised that the family had been trying to fix her rather than understand her.
s330: Research suggests extroverted children often have reward systems that respond more strongly to social contact, excitement and novelty. Talking and playing with others is how they recharge, just as quiet reading recharges an introvert. Ananya's temperament was partly inherited, perhaps from a lively grandmother, and was not bad behaviour. In a quiet household, her normal level of energy felt loud and overwhelming to the others, whose nervous systems settle faster with calm. When a child repeatedly hears that she is too much, she may begin to believe that her very self is a problem. That belief can grow into shame, people-pleasing or hiding. Children still need to learn self-control and kindness, but that growth works best when they first feel accepted for who they are.
s331: Her parents learned that Ananya was not too much, just different from them. Instead of asking her to shrink, they began to help her find good places for her energy and to teach her gentle self-control without shame.
s332: Replace the phrase too much with words like lively and joyful
s333: Plan daily outdoor play and time with friends
s334: Teach a simple quiet signal for moments that need calm
s335: Give her a role welcoming guests and leading family songs
s336: Let each family member share what recharges them
s337: Scripture shows that God delights in variety in His people. David danced before the LORD with all his might (2 Samuel 6:14), and when Michal despised him for it, David said, I will yet be more vile than thus (2 Samuel 6:22). Psalm 139:14 says, I will praise thee, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Proverbs 22:6 reminds parents to train up a child in the way he should go, which means paying attention to the child's own way and bent. Paul teaches that the body has many members, and the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee (1 Corinthians 12:21). In a family, the quiet ones and the lively ones belong together.
s338: God could have made every child a copy of their parents, but He chose variety instead. Extroverted children often bring warmth, courage and connection into a home. They pull quiet families outward and help them laugh and welcome others. Their energy is a raw gift that needs shaping, not crushing. God designed families to be places where different temperaments rub against each other and grow. The lively child learns patience, and the quiet parents learn joy. Through this, everyone becomes a little more like Christ, who was both deeply reflective and wonderfully warm with people.
s339: Psalm 139:14|I will praise thee, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made
s343: Change came slowly. Her parents still slipped into old phrases on tired days, and Ananya sometimes went over the top at family gatherings. But when they apologised and used the quiet signal, she responded more quickly. Her teacher reported that she now helps shy classmates join games. At home she talks just as much, but she no longer believes she is a problem.
s344: A lively child needs to be understood and shaped, not shamed into shrinking.
s345: God made some children quiet and some children loud and bubbly. Both are good, and every child can learn kindness and self-control.
s346: The Couple Who Fought About Saturdays
s347: Rohan, 33, and Meera, 31, a married couple in Bengaluru, Karnataka
s348: Every Friday night the same argument began. Rohan, an extrovert who worked from home all week, wanted to meet friends, visit cousins and go to a church picnic on Saturday. Meera, an introvert who spent all week teaching forty noisy children, wanted nothing more than a quiet day at home with tea and a book. You never want to do anything with me, Rohan would say. You never let me rest, Meera would reply. Rohan felt rejected and lonely. Meera felt guilty and drained. Soon they were spending weekends either at events where Meera was silent and tense, or at home where Rohan sulked on his phone. After one bitter fight, Meera cried, I think we are just too different to be happy. Rohan quietly wondered if she was right.
s349: Research suggests introverts and extroverts recharge in different ways. Meera's nervous system was already full after a week of classroom noise, so more social time felt like stress. Rohan's reward system responds more strongly to social contact, and after a week of working alone, his tank was nearly empty. Neither was wrong. Their needs were real and opposite. But each read the other's need as a message about love. Rohan heard I do not want you, and Meera heard you do not care about me. Both had grown up in families where love was measured by doing the same things together. Under stress, couples often fall into a pursue and withdraw pattern, which only deepens the gap.
s350: At a marriage course, they learned that their difference was a design to understand, not a flaw to fix. They began to talk about energy instead of blame, and to plan weekends that met both their needs.
s351: Each person rates their energy level on Friday night
s352: Plan one social event and one quiet block every weekend
s353: Rohan meets friends alone sometimes without guilt
s354: Meera joins one outing gladly and leaves when ready
s355: Say thank you for each sacrifice made for the other
s356: Scripture calls married people to serve one another in love. Philippians 2:4 says, Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. Paul writes, By love serve one another (Galatians 5:13). Peter tells husbands to dwell with their wives according to knowledge (1 Peter 3:7), which means taking time to understand how the other is made. Ecclesiastes 4:9 reminds us that two are better than one. Romans 15:7 says, Receive ye one another, as Christ also received us. Love does not demand that the other become like us. It makes room, gives way and seeks the good of the other, just as Christ did for us.
s357: God often brings opposites together, and research suggests many happy couples differ in temperament. An extrovert helps an introvert stay connected to community, while an introvert helps an extrovert slow down and go deeper. Like two hands with different shapes that fit together in prayer, their differences can make the marriage stronger. These differences also stretch both partners toward selfless love, which is part of how God grows Christlike character in marriage. What feels like a clash can become a classroom for humility, patience and grace.
s358: Philippians 2:4|Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others
s362: The new plan did not end every disagreement. Festival seasons and family weddings still pushed Meera past her limit, and Rohan still felt lonely some Sundays. But they now argued less and laughed more. Meera discovered she enjoyed small gatherings with two friends. Rohan began to look forward to their quiet Saturday mornings together. They learned to repair quickly when they slipped.
s363: When couples see their differences as design rather than rejection, they can plan a life that fits them both.
s364: Some people rest by being with friends and some rest by being quiet. A husband and wife can take turns and share, so both feel loved.
s366: Arjun, 16, a Class 11 student in Chennai, Tamil Nadu
s367: Arjun told everyone he was just an introvert. He avoided the school canteen, ate lunch in the library and never raised his hand in class, even when he knew the answer. When his youth group planned a trip, he made an excuse not to go. But inside, Arjun was not peacefully enjoying solitude. He longed to have friends and to join the cricket team. Before any class presentation, his heart raced, his hands sweated and he could not sleep for days. He was sure everyone would laugh at him. Once, when a teacher asked him to read aloud, his voice shook so much that he ran to the washroom. He told his mother he simply liked being alone, but at night he lay awake feeling lonely and ashamed.
s368: Introversion, shyness and social anxiety are not the same thing. Research suggests introversion is a temperament about energy, where a person prefers quieter settings but is not afraid of people. Shyness is a nervous discomfort in new social situations. Social anxiety is a stronger fear of being judged, which leads to avoidance and real distress. Arjun's alarm system, the amygdala, was firing in social situations as if he were in danger. Each time he avoided something, he felt relief, which taught his brain that avoidance was the right choice and made the fear grow. A harsh comment from a teacher in Class 6, when classmates laughed at his mistake, had left a deep mark. Calling himself introverted helped him hide the pain, but it also kept him from getting help.
